article.overview:
A lunar navigation receiver is an instrument that picks up radio signals from navigation satellites and uses them to estimate where a spacecraft or lander is, how fast it is moving and what time it is. On Earth, global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) such as GPS and Galileo support everything from phones to aircraft. The Moon has no equivalent service, so a receiver there would have to use signals from satellites orbiting Earth, roughly 330,000 to 430,000 km away. At that distance the signals are very weak and reach the Moon mainly through the weaker outer parts of the antenna beam.

The best-documented example is the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), a NASA and Italian Space Agency (ASI) payload that flew on Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 1 lander in early 2025. Its first results, published in March 2026 in the journal NAVIGATION, report tracking of Earth-based GNSS signals during the transfer to the Moon, in lunar orbit and on the lunar surface [1]. A second, planned example, the NaviMoon receiver for ESA's Lunar Pathfinder spacecraft, is described in the Physical Specifications section.
article.description:
A lunar navigation receiver typically consists of a radio antenna, a low-noise amplifier, a radio-frequency front end that converts the signal, a digital processor that tracks each satellite signal, and a precise clock. Each satellite broadcasts its position and a timestamp. The receiver measures how long each signal took to arrive and how its frequency shifted, then combines measurements from several satellites to compute a position, velocity and time solution, as a terrestrial GNSS receiver does [1]. The main engineering difference is signal strength. The flight signals measured by LuGRE were 7 to 12 dB weaker than the authors' simulation predicted for GPS L1 signals, which shows how sensitive lunar measurements are [1].

Lunar receivers are intended to give landers, rovers and orbiters a navigation and timing capability that does not depend entirely on Earth-based tracking stations, which need ground infrastructure. ESA's stated goal for GNSS-based navigation in lunar orbit is position accuracy better than 100 m, and ESA's Moonlight initiative aims at an operational lunar navigation infrastructure [3][4]. These are design goals and programme aims, not demonstrated performance.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The payload's purpose is technological and operational rather than geophysical. It tests whether Earth's GNSS signals can support positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) at the Moon [2]. LuGRE's stated objectives were to receive GNSS signals at the Moon, to demonstrate navigation and time estimation there, and to support the development of future lunar GNSS receivers [1]. Possible applications include: supporting landing and surface navigation for lunar missions, reducing dependence on ground tracking; providing a time reference for lunar spacecraft and surface assets; supporting navigation of orbiters and transfer spacecraft in cislunar space [3][4]; and providing measured datasets that can be used to design future lunar GNSS services. LuGRE's public data products were released in October 2025 [1].

These are proposed applications. Whether a given mission uses such a receiver depends on its design, and the sources reviewed do not describe an operational lunar GNSS service.
article.operating_principle: The receiver uses the same basic method as an Earth-based GNSS receiver. It measures the delay of each satellite signal (the pseudorange) and the Doppler shift of its carrier frequency, then solves for its own position, velocity and clock error. In the LuGRE design, a passive high-gain patch antenna array feeds a low-noise amplifier and a digital receiver built on a Xilinx Zynq 7000 system-on-chip with an Analog Devices AD9361 radio front end. The receiver tracks GPS and Galileo signals on the L1/E1 and L5/E5a frequencies [1]. The LuGRE authors report that code (pseudorange) measurement noise was about two orders of magnitude higher than carrier-phase noise, and that the receiver's clock drift was strongly correlated with its temperature [1].
article.scientific_importance: The Moon currently has no operational satellite navigation service, and lunar missions depend on Earth-based tracking and onboard sensors. Demonstrating GNSS reception at lunar distances is a technical precondition for more autonomous lunar spacecraft navigation [1][3]. LuGRE's dataset gives researchers measured signal characteristics at lunar distances rather than only modelled values [1]. The scientific value is mainly metrological and engineering: the measurements show how weak and how available these signals are at the Moon, which directly constrains receiver and service design.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar navigation receiver. Mass, power, antenna and clock requirements depend on the signal bands used, the accuracy target and the host spacecraft. The two examples below are not directly comparable. The first is a flown instrument with published hardware figures. The second is a planned receiver whose flight specifications were not verified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), flown on Blue Ghost Mission 1
examples.status: Flown in 2025 on Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 1 lunar lander, as a NASA and ASI payload under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) Task Order 19D [1][2].
examples.total_payload_mass_note: Less than 5 kg for the flight model, per [1].
examples.receiver_mass_note: A receiver-only mass of 1.3 kg appears in a secondary search summary but was not confirmed in the primary paper and is not used here.
examples.receiver: Qascom QN400-SPACE, in two cold-redundant units (primary and secondary), built on a Xilinx Zynq 7000 system-on-chip with an Analog Devices AD9361 radio front end.
examples.antenna: Passive L-band 3 x 3 planar array with right-hand circular polarisation. Peak boresight gain 15.35 dBic at L1/E1 (half-power beamwidth 12 degrees) and 14.56 dBic at L5/E5 (half-power beamwidth 16 degrees).
examples.low_noise_amplifier: Gain 41.5 dB at L1/E1 and 44.2 dB at L5/E5; noise figure 0.8 dB at L1 and 1.3 dB at L5.
examples.tracking_channels_note: The number of tracking channels is not stated in the text reviewed.
examples.clock: Commercial VCTCXO oscillator with a start-up clock-drift transient, described as typically lasting 10 to 15 minutes.
key_flight_results: 16 in-flight operations: two commissioning, nine during Earth-phasing and five in lunar orbit.
Tracking of GPS and Galileo signals; the longest-range signal was from a Galileo satellite at about 433,220 km.
First lunar-surface navigation fix on 3 March 2025 at about 356,237 km from Earth.
More than 95 hours of surface operation, with nearly 93 hours in real-time processing mode.

examples.name: NaviMoon receiver for ESA's Lunar Pathfinder (planned)
examples.status: Planned and not flown in the sources reviewed. NaviMoon is a high-sensitivity variant of SpacePNT's NAVILEO spaceborne GNSS receiver, developed for ESA and intended for Surrey Satellite Technology's Lunar Pathfinder spacecraft, which would carry it into lunar orbit [3].
examples.design_goal_position_accuracy_m: Better than 100 m in lunar orbit (ESA design goal) [3].
examples.launch_status_note: A 2023 report said the flight payload was ready for integration and had been targeted for a late-2025 launch [3]. A third-party launch tracker lists a no-earlier-than 2027 window [5], which should be checked against an official update.
examples.dimensions_and_antenna: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified dimensions were found for the LuGRE receiver or for the planned NaviMoon receiver. The LuGRE payload's antenna and low-noise amplifier were mounted on the lander at locations shown in the paper's figures [1], but the sources reviewed do not give a dimensional drawing with values. A new receiver's dimensions would need to be set by its antenna aperture, thermal design and mounting requirements.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: For spacecraft engineering, mass is normally expressed in kilograms. The LuGRE flight-model total payload is reported as less than 5 kg [1]. The receiver-only mass is not confirmed in the primary paper reviewed. No mass is verified for the NaviMoon receiver. Mass affects launch requirements and the design of the host spacecraft, so the total payload mass should be used when assessing transport compatibility.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LuGRE's maximum operational power is 14 W [1]. The power source is the lander's supply, and the article reviewed does not describe a separate payload power system. No power figure is verified for NaviMoon.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar receiver must work without an atmosphere, through large surface temperature swings and under radiation and dust exposure. LuGRE's measurements show that the clock and receiver temperature are closely linked, so thermal control of the oscillator and electronics matters for measurement quality [1]. Antenna pointing is also critical. LuGRE's antenna had to face Earth, and its measured surface pointing error met a 1 degree requirement with a wide margin [1]. Mission operations were limited in number and duration to protect the lander's attitude-control resources, and surface operations were paused during high-heating periods near lunar noon [1]. From the Moon, the Earth-based GNSS constellations occupy less than 10 degrees of sky, which limits satellite geometry [2].
article.limitations: Earth-based GNSS signals reach the Moon mainly through weak side lobes. The lower-than-expected signal level pushed most side-lobe signals below the acquisition threshold, which reduced availability [1]. The satellites are confined to a small part of the sky seen from the Moon [2], which affects geometry, accuracy and availability. The authors describe the 7 to 12 dB C/N0 shortfall as a peculiarity of this mission, and its root causes were still under investigation at the time of publication [1]. Clock drift correlated with receiver temperature, and the oscillator showed a start-up transient [1]. One mission's results do not establish a general performance guarantee for future receivers.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: LuGRE was carried as a payload on the Blue Ghost Mission 1 lunar lander and was not deployed by a separate mechanism. The planned NaviMoon receiver would instead fly on an orbiting spacecraft, Lunar Pathfinder, which would reach lunar orbit on a transfer vehicle [3][5].
transportation_process: LuGRE: integrated on the Blue Ghost Mission 1 lander, with its antenna, low-noise amplifier and receiver mounted on the lander [1].
LuGRE: launched on 15 January 2025, landed on 2 March 2025 and ended operations on 16 March 2025 [1].
NaviMoon (planned): to be integrated into the Lunar Pathfinder spacecraft, launched on a transfer vehicle and inserted into lunar orbit [3][5]. Schedule not verified.
No verified interface data (mass, power, pointing and data requirements) were found for Lunar Pathfinder, so no compatibility with a specific lander or transfer vehicle can be asserted.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: LuGRE did not use a deployment mechanism. Its antenna and electronics were fixed to the lander, and operations were scheduled to protect the lander's attitude-control resources [1]. NASA's pre-flight page described surface operation for up to two weeks [2], but the flight data show more than 95 hours of surface operation [1].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LuGRE, flown on Blue Ghost Mission 1 in 2025, is the best-documented lunar example in the sources reviewed [1]. The NaviMoon receiver on Lunar Pathfinder is a planned follow-on [3][5].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: LuGRE's integration is documented only for Blue Ghost Mission 1. A future receiver's compatibility with a particular lander would need to be assessed using its mass, dimensions, mounting points, antenna field of view, power, thermal and pointing requirements and data interfaces. It should not be assigned to a specific lander until those requirements have been compared with verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: LuGRE is the first NASA and ASI demonstration of GNSS reception at the Moon documented in a peer-reviewed article, published in March 2026 [1]. Secondary coverage describes it as the first known demonstration of acquiring Earth-based GNSS signals at the Moon. That priority claim was not checked against a primary source beyond the paper's title. The planned NaviMoon receiver and ESA's Moonlight initiative are the next steps that the sources identify for lunar GNSS [3][4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Receiver hardware:** the receiver-only mass, the number of tracking channels and the full dimensions were not confirmed in the primary text reviewed. The receiver-only mass of 1.3 kg in a secondary summary was excluded.
- **Distances:** secondary summaries gave distances of about 395,900 km and 362,100 km, which differ from the paper's figures. This article uses the paper's values, which were 390,416 km maximum tracked distance in lunar orbit and 356,237 km for the first surface fix.
- **Navigation accuracy:** the text reviewed covered only the first part of the paper. Surface position accuracy values, the availability analysis and the lessons-learned section were not reviewed, so no surface accuracy figure is given.
- **Pre-flight source:** the NASA Goddard page was last updated on 29 April 2025 and describes pre-flight plans. Its two-week surface duration is superseded by the flight data.
- **Artist's concept:** the image shows an artist's concept, not flight hardware or a photograph from the Moon. The direct image URL was taken from the source page and not independently opened.
- **NaviMoon:** no verified flight specifications. The launch window comes from a single third-party tracker [5], and references [3] to [5] were identified from search results and were not opened in full.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Only one image is included. It is an artist's concept from the NASA Goddard LuGRE page, not a photograph of flight hardware. No verified photograph or official image asset of the LuGRE receiver or of the NaviMoon receiver was found in the sources reviewed.

Primary-source coverage is partial. The LuGRE NAVIGATION paper was read only for its first ~100,000 of ~193,000 characters. Surface position accuracy, availability (Figure 22), tracking-channel count and the lessons-learned section are not verified.
Distance figures conflict across sources. Secondary summaries gave about 395,900 km and 362,100 km. The paper's values (390,416 km and 356,237 km) are used.
The LuGRE receiver-only mass of 1.3 kg appears only in a secondary search summary and is excluded. The paper gives a total payload mass of less than 5 kg.
NaviMoon / Lunar Pathfinder: no verified flight specifications, and the launch window (no earlier than 2027) comes from a single third-party tracker. Sources [3] to [5] were not opened in full.
The 'first GNSS reception at the Moon' priority claim comes from secondary coverage and was not checked against a primary source beyond the paper's title.
The NASA Goddard LuGRE page is a pre-flight page and was last updated 2025-04-29. Its two-week surface duration is superseded by the flight figures in [1].
